references.text: Later in the same chapter, the disciples themselves tell how the women came and told them about the empty tomb: [ref:Luk 24:22-24|Luke 24:22-24].
In Matthew's account, the women at the tomb are likewise told to go and tell the disciples about the resurrection: [ref:Matt 28:8|Matthew 28:8].
Mark tells of Mary Magdalene going and telling those who had been with Jesus, but they did not believe her: [ref:Mark 16:10-11|Mark 16:10-11].
In John's account, Mary Magdalene goes to the disciples and tells them that she has seen the Lord: [ref:Joh 20:18|John 20:18].
The following verse names the women who brought the message and states that the disciples did not believe them: [ref:Luk 24:10-11|Luke 24:10-11].

The travelers from Emmaus returned to the eleven and told what they had experienced, confirming that "the eleven" was the fixed designation for the group of disciples after Judas' departure: [ref:Luk 24:33-35|Luke 24:33-35].
The Acts of the Apostles confirms that there were only eleven apostles after Judas' fall, until Matthias was chosen: [ref:Apg 1:26|Acts 1:26].
Luke had earlier mentioned women who followed Jesus and served him, including Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Susanna – the same ones who now bring news from the tomb: [ref:Luk 8:2-3|Luke 8:2-3].

The women who accompanied him from Galilee noticed the tomb and returned to prepare fragrant spices – this is the direct background for why they now return from the tomb with the message: [ref:Luk 23:55-56|Luke 23:55-56].
